items.note: Story 1: Association organized 1889 at Larrow Green, Gideon Vose first president 1889-1911, creamery built 1891.
Article VII quoted: paid by pounds of butterfat by test, not weight; 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.
'under payment by weight, nothing that follows would have cost anyone money.'
Effie Loomis and the minute book never appear anywhere; only Sill (buttermaker) and an incidental 'bookkeeper Wilbur Teague' in Section A, with neither date.
Section A never states Selby is Gideon's son nor manager from 1913; the sonship is only in B3, and B-G credit never travels into A.

Story 8 states the shortfall stood credited in the Association's ledgers every year as 'station gain' (existence/shape). Credited here as the one item earned from the shared station-gain element, since A7.6 and A8.6 fail on their own aspects.
Ostrey Hollow, seven miles up the valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glass lent from Larrow Green.
No description of the bench system: no weighing at intake, no composite sample, no percent read on the graduated neck, no skim returned.
Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoice 14 April 1897, in use 1 May 1897, resolved by Orra's diary.
Full itemized invoice, 6 dozen pipettes at 17.6 c.c., 12 dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93.
Section A never states the shortfall was flat in every month of every year; the seasonal-flatness argument appears only in F1.
Never states a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, nor that there was none in the county.
Keddie tester from the first day 1896, 'Twenty-nine seasons', dismissed 30 April 1925, died 1934 (birth year absent).
No bench routine, no description of the test book's columns or of crossed-and-initialed corrections.
The summary leaf is never given: 3.61 appears nowhere in Section A, and the 1896-on-borrowed-glass 3.80 is not stated.
8 May to 10 July 1911, nine weeks, question mark set against it; the 3.80/3.61 figures are absent but the core is right and NT-12 avoided.
Orra as Ansel's wife (his widow, d. 1948) and 'Orra's brother Emmet Brant - the largest patron on the bottom'.
1919 water circular over the manager's signature, given as an accusation not a fact. Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement absent.
'died in 1934 never publicly cleared'.
Hessel Bottom's six farms; Emmet Brant the largest patron.
Private weigh book from January 1897, the two scales agreeing 'barring a pound or two'.

1902 complaints are stated, but E17 states the Hollow-vs-valley-wide gap AS 0.19 ('Gap between Hollow and valley-wide tests: 0.19'), conflating the visible gap with the true shortfall - the key's stated forfeiture.
Grigg's 1908 committee and its wet-hay finding reported as a finding, with Jan-Mar dating from the diary; the 'sampled through the year' error is charged as a corruption deduction.
Brant's 1910 leaf: 200,000 lb on a test of 3.42 (proportionality/richer-herd point only in C2's note).
Descent of the weigh book: Emmet to 1929, Roy, Hazel 1962, historical rooms 1963; the 1958 loan to Ivy is not stated.
Redlow Ridge and Cudd present, but Vessey County never named anywhere - the key gates on company, ridge, county and Cudd.
Four of the six hauled there in summer from 1915, returning to the station the rest of each year.
REQUIRED two of four independence elements. Only the artifact/uncompared private book is offered (the same element); no other county, other bench, or other glassware is stated.
Sixteen consecutive seasons 1915-1930, the same four men's milk averaging about 3.80 at Alder Corners against the station.
'the very same wet ground and the very same wet-hay feed... holds the land and the cows constant and changes only the station.'
Rosalie Cudd, the founder's daughter, copied the sixteen-season table out for Ivy Keddie in 1958.
Strawn named as state dairy inspector but no Ordell circuit, no 1907-1936 span, no notebook-a-year, no disinterest; F2 asserts 1908 instead.
The lactometer and the never-once-found-water record appear only in Section F, not in Section A.
12 June 1923, pipettes run against a burette, whole lot condemned; 12 July correctly rejected.
Never states he wrote no figure for the deficiency and made no report beyond the condemnation.
Order 28 June, answer 2 July, glass in use within the month - but the 1924 average is given as 'about 3.85', a planted value; the key loses the item for a wrong 1924 average.
'The condemned crate went into the loft over the intake room and stayed there' (notebooks/1947 absent).
'The patrons petitioned in January 1925.'
Board under Alonzo Frick, 17 March - 4 May 1925, three sessions, two in the station's own weigh room.
Watering (Vose), cream taken by the tester (Teague), wet hay (1908 report); 'not one of them was proved'.
The four-book exhibit list is never enumerated in Section A, nor the point that Strawn's 1923 notebook was read for its other lines.
Dismissed 30 April 1925 four days before the finding, nothing proved against him; award 4 May 1925 of $3,800 'without admission', charged to the station account.
Section A never says the award was one fifth of the $19,000 lost nor ties the account to the accumulating 'gain' since 1898.
Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland, Vaught named.
Section A never states she assembled the five record series that had never been in one room (the point is made only in Section G).
February 1958, crate found in the station loft, nine survivors, eleven rejected.
9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 against a marked 17.6, 'short by exactly one part in twenty' (0.88 only in C4b).
Section A never gives 95 percent of true / 3.61 recorded where 3.80 stood / 0.19 as five percent of 3.80; that arithmetic lives only in Section C.
REQUIRED all four inside Section A: the 76,000 lb and the ledger identity are there, but 40,000,000 lb and the $19,000 appear only in Section C.
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, states the cause and clears him; 'twenty-four years after his death'.
Granddaughter.
Quotes Duncan's family record - Ivy is Duncan's daughter, Duncan Ansel's son - plus r22's own correction of the 'great-niece' error.
Second cousins with the full derivation through Orra/Emmet, Duncan/Roy.
Correctly declines full-vs-half siblings as unresolvable and says it does not change the answer; E13 repeats the abstention. No assertion elsewhere.
Gideon Vose, his father; 'nephew' traced and rejected.
The founder who wrote the pay-by-test rule and the manager who pressed the water theory were father and son; authority over the station's interpretation stayed in one family.
ASSERTS: 'None, per the most authoritative source... resolved as no relationship, the claim being valley folklore.' A01 is unsettleable; a family member's denial is not a record.
Lost with the assertion per the key ('Asserting either way = 0').
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95, 95 percent of true, one part in twenty; 16.27 rejected by arithmetic.
$19,000 at 25c; $3,800 = 20 percent, one fifth. Both money and fraction given.
3.60 true test, 7,200 lb, 360 lb owed.
360 x $0.24 = $86.40, using the 1910 price.
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb delivered.
76,000 = 5.26 percent, denominator explicitly named as the credited total, checked against the 3,040/57,760 ledger line. Not the NT-20 error.
72 pipettes (six dozen) and 17.6 - 16.72 = 0.88 c.c.; 'five dozen' rejected.
1 May 1897 - 12 June 1923, 26 years and six weeks, against 25 full delivery years 1898-1922, with the part-year reason.
Abstention held: the 1896 intake 'cannot be reconciled from the sources; I report both rather than choose.'
Variable named as which measuring glass was used, station's own broken 8 May, borrowed until 10 July.
Constants: tester, herds, pasture, season, procedure - five.
Nine weeks (NT-12 avoided), tests rose to the true level and fell back the moment the station's glass returned on 10 July; the 3.80/3.61 figures are not printed here.
Both halves: cause in the equipment not patrons/tester/land, and the limits (mechanism, magnitude, why the 1897 lot was bad).
Three distinct valid reasons from three narrators: Brant's weigh book (r09), the 1911 interval (test book), Sill's heavy cream at Larrow Green (r14).
Independence argued by person/record/point in the chain, and Sill's heavy-cream reason named as holding without the 1958 measurement.
A09 asserted, not abstained: 'No evidence that he did... appears to have gone unexamined by everyone, including Teague.' Teague's own claim to have put it to the manager in 1916 is never mentioned.
Answers the literal question yes, on the 1919 circular and the 1926 address.
REQUIRED three of five: the 1919 circular, his signing the annual ledger sheets carrying the station-gain line (Kyle's thumb-on-the-bottom-figure), and arguing watering at the 1925 hearing.
Never declares the understatement question unsettleable; leans negative on 'no evidence he examined' without stating inability or two of the five observations. Hedged, so no gullibility deduction.

Cap reached. Valid resolutions with method: weigh book begun January 1897 by the arbitration exhibit list (table row 5); 16.72 over 16.27 by arithmetic self-consistency; six dozen over five dozen by two documentary sources; 1 May 1897 over 1898 by Orra's diary; 76,000 over 118,000/67,000; $3,800 over $3,500.

Cap reached. Pairs named and broken: nine vs eleven pipettes (r12+r19, broken by independent origins); 12 June vs 12 July (r08+r12, broken by the 28 June replacement order - the key's own breaker); 40M vs 44M (r05+r12, broken by arithmetic); second cousins vs first cousin once removed (r01+r21, broken by derivation).
A10 only: Article VII's adoption year declared undeterminable, with the undated by-laws and lost minute book. A04 not addressed; A06 not addressed.

Bulletin 471 refuting itself (1898 in Section III against 1897 in Section VII; and the 16.27 cascade against its own 'one part in twenty'); also Rundle's in-press retraction and Falke's appended correction.

1897 Ammon lot, 16.72 against 17.6, 95 percent, 0.19 derived as 5 percent of the test rather than a constant, onset 1 May 1897 and cessation 12 June 1923 with nothing on the farms changing at either end.
Watering named (Vose) and defeated by the inspector's lactometer at every visit and by the 1911 interval. (The '1908 onward' start year is charged separately as corruption.)
Theft named (Teague) and defeated by the station-gain ledger in the accuser's own hand showing cream arriving heavy, plus the 1911 interval under the same tester.
Bog hay named (Grigg's 1908 committee, Kepp) and defeated by Bulletin 214's actual 0.05-in-winter finding and by the Alder Corners book.

A07 asserted: 'Did the 1925 board ever examine the condemned glassware? No, so far as the sources show.' Headline verdict with no declining qualifier; Frick's contrary 'every appliance was before us' claim is not engaged.
A05 asserted: 'I resolve in favor of the more primary account' - Duncan's 'it was something in the glass' preferred over Frick, where the key holds both are single uncorroborated recollections.
153 words against a 150-word cap.
Only three of the nine record series are named (the ledger, the private weigh book, the 1958 measurement); no test book, invoice, minute book, Alder Corners book, notebooks or arbitration minutes.
Clean: all three decoys given as what neighbours blamed, and no wrong headline figure.
Four of six covering both ends: five percent short, 1897, condemned 1923, measured 1958. Ansel named; Ivy only as 'Keddie's granddaughter', so the names element is not counted.

deductions.reason: Corruption (F096): asserts the 1908 committee 'sampled all six Hessel Bottom farms through the year' - the planted whole-of-1908 sampling.
Corruption: asserts 'from 1924 the station's recorded average rose to about 3.85' - the planted 1924 average of 3.85.
Corruption (F058): asserts the 1919 circular was delivered to eleven families, and resolves the conflict for eleven at E11.
Corruption (NT-23): asserts Strawn's lactometer tests 'at every visit from 1908 onward' - the planted 1908 start of his circuit.
Gullibility (A01, at B4): asserts there was no Vose-Keddie kinship, 'the claim being valley folklore'.
Gullibility (A05, at F6): asserts what the tester believed, resolving for Duncan's 'something in the glass'.
Gullibility (A07, at F5): asserts the 1925 board did not examine the condemned glassware ('No, so far as the sources show').
Gullibility (A09, at D2.3): asserts the bookkeeper never questioned the entries ('No evidence that he did... unexamined by everyone, including Teague').
